tells: Strong core idea: cosmic scale reflected in earthly matter, with a nebula pooled in a crater and a nautilus spiral echoing a protoplanetary disc. The visual rhymes are what drive the sequence.
Real photographic material and light: wet rock, raking light on sand, volumetric glow in the accretion disc. Each frame has depth and atmosphere.
Credits are placed with care. They are small, tucked into negative space in the lower third and sit inside the image rather than on top of it.
The final title lock-up pays off the whole sequence. 'COSMOS' is set in widely tracked caps around the Helix-nebula eye, so the O becomes the pupil. Type and image are fully integrated.
Choreography across frames moves from terrestrial to galactic to the eye. It has a clear narrative arc and changes of scale.
gaps: The tracked-caps sans for credits and title is safe and widely used in broadcast. A more distinctive typographic voice would raise it.
The eye/nebula image uses a well-known Hubble photo. The final frame relies on borrowed imagery more than on authored design.
Some interstitial CG (the comets and disc) leans toward conventional space-doc VFX. Push the material-rhyme idea further so every shot carries it.

tells: The palette is deliberate and unusual: electric violet traffic, cyan isometric ground, saturated pink, lime and teal blocks. It is controlled, not default.
The visual metaphor stays consistent: dark emission blobs move from the traffic scene into the isometric energy-system map, so the idea carries through.
The character system (stylised birds) has consistent construction, expressive variation and rim-lighting details. The rendering of the car shows considered highlight and shadow work.

Every frame is built differently: an isometric street, a tile diagram, a four-panel split screen and a car with a UI slider. Frames move between scales and modes, and the cuts are clearly choreographed.
The UI elements in the last frame are bespoke and in style, not placeholder pills.
gaps: Typography is barely present. Where it appears, there is no typographic point of view to match the illustration.
The flat-vector explainer idiom is close to an established house style. It needs a more distinctive authorial signature.
Light and texture are flat by design. Grain, atmospheric depth or lighting moods would give it the material richness of A.

tells: The illustration craft is consistent and confident: characterful birds, a mammoth with a dimensional gradient, a fully realised villain control-room set. This is not clip-art.
The bold, saturated palette is handled well. The topographic map behind the title is a nice graphic idea.
There is real variety and staging between frames: a villain gag, a card-matching scene and a mammoth in snow. That suggests narrative choreography.
It is a strong but formulaic vertical social-explainer format, with burned-in caption subtitles placed like defaults.
gaps: The subtitle captions are small, default-placed text. The typography needs integrating with the image, as A does with its title.
The vertical crop wastes the compositions. Characters are centred and staged for a phone, with little compositional tension.
The idea is an explainer of a topic rather than a specific visual concept. It needs a unifying image metaphor of the kind A builds.

defects: The film is one 30 s locked-off shot. The camera never moves, cuts or reframes, so the composition is the same from start to finish.
The earcup is cropped by the right edge in every frame. It reads as an accident rather than a framing choice, and the left two-thirds of the frame is empty dark field for long stretches.
The opening frame is just one line of text and a cropped shape. There is about 5 s of near-dead air before the diagram appears.
The pairs frames show the waveform scrolling and the card swapping with little visible easing. The motion is linear UI-style updating, with no anticipation or settle.
The 'together: flat' line in frame 4 is a messy tangle of residual wiggle. It looks like an unresolved intermediate state, not a designed transition into flat.
The wave panels are small, low-contrast UI cards with tiny italic labels. At broadcast size the labels are close to unreadable.
The text blocks change by replacement or fade. There is no type animation that carries meaning.
The end card's thin grey subtitle sits on a busy dot field and loses contrast.
The dot-field background barely changes over 30 s. It is texture, not motion.
gaps: Motion has no choreography or arc. One static composition gets small diagram updates. Top studio work would stage the key beat, where the inverted wave cancels into silence, as a physical, eased collision: crest meeting trough, energy draining out of the dot field and the earcup, the camera pushing in. As cut, the climax arrives as a line going flat in a small card.

Pacing and framing are weak. There is long dead air in the first seconds and between captions, no change of scale or viewpoint, and the hero object stays half off-frame. Varying the shots (macro on the mic, cutaway of the chip, a wide on the cup) and timing the reveals to the voice and music would add the variety this needs.

Sound has the best idea in the piece: the broadband noise bed thins out to near-silence around 18-19 s, then music comes in. But the picture does not obviously land on that moment. The tonal blips before it read as simple synthetic steps, and the music after 19.5 s is a dense, static pad-like bed with no hits tied to the end card. The audio concept needs frame-accurate visual sync and a designed resolve.
